transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

Well, Doctor, I... I suppose I'm here because my regular doctor thought it would be a good idea for me to talk to someone, but really, the core of it is that I am just completely exhausted trying to get someone, anyone, to actually take me seriously. I’ve been a computer support specialist for... gosh, going on thirty-five years now. I have my bachelor's degree, I know how these enterprise systems operate on the backend, I've built half of them. But for over a year now—fourteen months exactly, ever since the third quarter of last year—there has been this situation at work. 

They rolled out this new ticket rotation protocol and these constant, highly specific security audits. On paper, they claim it's for compliance, but I know exactly what's going on. They are systematically using the ticket routing and these audits to build a paper trail against me. I can see the way the high-priority, impossible-to-resolve tickets are being artificially diverted into my specific queue right before the audit sweeps run. It's designed to make my metrics look terrible. I’ve tried to show the evidence to management, I've sat in their offices and explained the routing logic and the server loads, but they just... they just keep pulling up these sanitized system logs, pointing at the screen, and telling me, "Oh, it's just company policy, everyone is subject to the same rotation." 

But it's not just policy! If you actually look at the timestamps and the IP assignments, it is mathematically impossible for it to be a random distribution. It is a targeted effort to manufacture a reason to terminate me, and it is incredibly frustrating that management just smiles and lies to my face about the logs while my entire career is on the line. So, I guess I'm here because the stress of nobody listening to the facts is starting to wear me down.
Have you tended to be suspicious or mistrustful of other people in many areas of your life, not just at work?

No, no, not at all. That’s the thing, Doctor, that’s what makes this whole situation so incredibly baffling to me, and frankly, a bit insulting when my regular doctor implied I might be... well, you know. I’m not some paranoid guy sitting in a dark room jumping at shadows. I’ve lived in the same neighborhood for twenty-two years. I know all my neighbors. Bob and Linda next door, we share a property line and we’ve never had a single dispute, not even when their big oak tree dropped branches all over my driveway after that storm back in '18. I just got my chainsaw and helped him cut it up. I’m actually on the neighborhood HOA board, for heaven's sake, and I handle the community newsletter's formatting. 

I trust the people in my life. My kids—my daughter just had her first baby, actually, a little girl—we couldn't be closer. I have guys I’ve been playing poker with every other Thursday since the late nineties. I don't look at them across the table and think they're trying to cheat me. I don't go to the grocery store and think the cashier is out to get me or shortchanging me. I am a perfectly reasonable, trusting person in literally every other aspect of my life. I base my trust on evidence, on how people treat me in reality. 

And I think... I really think that’s exactly why this work thing is so glaring! Because I'm not making it up out of some general mistrust of humanity. I’m looking at the actual server logs, the raw data. If my poker buddies started dealing from the bottom of the deck and I had a mathematical breakdown of the card distribution proving it, I'd call them out too! So no, I don't have a problem trusting people. I have a problem with a very specific group of middle managers who are actively manipulating an enterprise ticketing system to force me out, and I just want someone to look at the actual routing rules instead of treating me like I'm crazy.
Do you ever believe that people outside of work are also specifically trying to harm or target you?

No, no, absolutely not. I mean, why would they? That’s exactly what I was trying to explain about my poker buddies and my neighbors. Outside of that building, my life is completely... normal. It’s boring, even! I go to the grocery store, I get my coffee at the same little shop on the corner of 4th and Elm—the barista there, Sarah, she’s a sweetheart, always remembers I like a little extra room for cream—and I never once think anyone out there is following me or trying to ruin my life. 

It’s just... it’s isolated to the office. Because that’s where the motive is, right? The people at the grocery store don't care about my pension or my salary band. They don't have a vested interest in replacing a senior tech with two junior guys they can pay half as much. But the management at work? They do. And that’s what’s so incredibly frustrating about this whole process, this whole... talking to doctors thing. Because you ask me if I think people outside of work are targeting me, and I say no, because they aren't, but it feels like the fact that I'm only seeing this at work is somehow being used to say, "Oh, well, it must be in his head." But it's not! It’s just that the threat is localized to the environment where the threat actually exists! 

I don't walk around thinking the mailman is reading my letters. I don't think the cars behind me on the highway are tailing me. I just know, for an absolute, verifiable fact, that my direct supervisor and the compliance team are manipulating the load balancer on the ticketing system. That’s it. It begins and ends at the corporate firewall. So, no, nobody outside of work is bothering me. I just want to be left alone to do my job, the job I've been doing perfectly well for three and a half decades, without having to constantly monitor my own queue just to prove I'm not crazy.
Have you ever considered that your supervisor and the compliance team might not be targeting you, even a little?

Considered it? Doctor, I... look, I’m a rational man. I troubleshoot complex enterprise network systems for a living. The very first step in my job—the very first thing you are trained to do when a server goes down or a routing error pops up—is you ask yourself, "Is this a fluke? Is it user error? Is it just a statistical anomaly?" So yes, absolutely, in the beginning, I asked myself that. Back in, say, month one or two of this whole ordeal, I tried to give them the benefit of the doubt. I thought maybe the algorithm was just poorly written.

But I can't just ignore the data when it keeps piling up, month after month. Like I was saying when we first started talking, I have been dealing with this for over a year now. I am just so incredibly burnt out trying to get someone, anyone, to take this seriously. I didn't just jump to conclusions out of nowhere. But when you sit there and watch the new ticket rotation consistently, mathematically dump the most toxic, unresolvable issues into your specific queue right before the security audits hit... well, you do the math. They are using those audits and that rotation to build a paper trail against me at work, plain and simple. It's a manufactured trail of incompetence, designed to look like I'm failing to meet my service level agreements.

And it's maddening, Doctor, it really is, because I *have* tried to play devil's advocate with myself. I go into management's office, genuinely hoping that they can prove me wrong. I want them to show me a legitimate load-balancing configuration that explains why my queue is getting hammered. I practically beg them to explain the logic to me. But instead, they just pull up those same sanitized, high-level logs—the ones that conveniently strip out the IP assignments and the microsecond timestamps—they point at the screen, give me this patronizing little smile, and say, "Oh, it’s just policy. The rotation is random, the audits are standard company policy." 

They just keep showing me those useless, filtered logs and repeating the company line while they quietly build their case to terminate me. So, have I considered they might not be targeting me? Sure, I considered it a year ago. But I'm an engineer. I follow the facts. And the facts say that this isn't some harmless policy, it's a deliberate, targeted campaign. I just cannot fathom why nobody else is willing to look past the corporate double-speak, look at the actual routing rules, and see what is so obviously happening right in front of them.
Has anyone at work ever directly told you, in words, that they are trying to target or set you up?

Well, no, of course not. I mean, think about it, Doctor. Nobody is going to just come right out and say, "Hey, we're actively trying to set you up so we can fire you." That would be corporate suicide! Human Resources would have an absolute field day with a statement like that. The whole point of doing it through the backend systems is plausible deniability. They don't need to say it to my face because they are making the system do the dirty work for them.

And honestly, that... that right there is the exact reason I’m here talking to you right now. Because for over a year now—fourteen months and a couple of weeks, if we want to get specific—I’ve been trying, just absolutely exhausting myself, trying to get someone, anyone, to take this seriously. I need someone to look at the facts and see that the new ticket rotation and these relentless security audits are being used specifically to build a paper trail against me at work. It's a manufactured history of failure, designed to look legitimate on paper. 

But they'll never admit it out loud. Whenever I try to force the issue, whenever I march in there and demand a real explanation for why my queue is flooded with unsolvable legacy server errors right before an audit, management just does what they always do. Like I said, they keep showing me those same sanitized, filtered logs, pointing at the screen, and saying it’s just policy. "Oh, it's just standard policy, it's just the algorithm, nothing personal." They hide behind the word "policy" so they never have to actually say the words "we are targeting you." But I know what they're doing. The paper trail they are building does all the talking they need.
Do you believe your supervisor or the team is using any unusual powers or technology beyond normal workplace systems to target you?

Unusual powers? Like... what, telepathy? Mind reading? No, no, no. Doctor, you're—look, you're missing the point entirely if you think I'm sitting here talking about science fiction or, or magic. I'm a computer support specialist, I deal in reality. I deal in hardware, software, TCP/IP protocols. They don't need any sort of... supervillain technology to do this. That's the whole tragedy of it! They are just using the standard, everyday workplace systems that we all log into every single morning at 8:00 AM. 

Think about it. If you have root access, or even just high-level administrative privileges on the enterprise ticketing software—which my supervisor absolutely does, by the way, he requested elevated permissions back in 2019 during the big server migration—if you have that access, you don't need unusual powers. You just need to write a simple script. A basic SQL query or a modified routing rule on the load balancer. It's incredibly mundane technology. It's just... it's just drop-down menus and checkboxes on the backend that dictate where a support ticket goes. 

I mean, why would they invent some crazy new technology when the existing infrastructure is practically designed to be manipulated if you know where to look? They just go into the admin console, tweak the round-robin distribution settings, and boom, suddenly the guy they want to force into early retirement is drowning in severity-one legacy server crashes. It's all right there in the standard IT toolkit. No mind reading, no secret spy gadgets, no... whatever else people might come up with. Just plain, boring, everyday corporate software, weaponized by people who know exactly how to use the system's own rules against me. 

That's what makes it so completely impossible to fight, because to HR, or to anyone else who doesn't understand network architecture, it just looks like the system functioning normally. They don't see the strings being pulled. So, no, no unusual powers. Just standard admin rights and a complete lack of ethics.
Have you ever heard, seen, or otherwise sensed anything that other people couldn’t?

Heard or seen things? Like... like hallucinations? No. No, absolutely not. I know exactly what you're getting at with a question like that, Doctor, but you have to understand, I am a very grounded person. I'm sixty years old, and I've spent my entire adult life—literally decades, going all the way back to the early days of Novell NetWare and token ring networks—working with concrete, verifiable data. Ones and zeros. Either a packet reaches its destination or it drops. There is no room for imagination in my line of work. 

So no, I don't hear voices whispering to me from the server racks, and I don't see things that aren't there. Everything I am seeing, everything I'm experiencing at that office, is entirely physical and documented. It's digital, sure, but it is real. It is right there on the dual monitors at my desk. Anyone could see it! If you came to my cubicle right now and I pulled up the raw server logs, you would see the exact same timestamps and the exact same manipulated ticket assignments that I see. The problem isn't that I'm seeing things other people *can't* see, Doctor, it's that I'm looking at things other people *refuse* to look at. 

I mean, I get why you ask. I really do. It's your job to rule things out, run down your clinical checklist, make sure the guy sitting across from you hasn't completely lost his grip on reality. I respect the troubleshooting process, I do the same thing with hardware. But my senses are perfectly fine. I get my vision checked every single year—you absolutely have to when you stare at screens for ten, twelve hours a day, the blue light and the eye strain alone will ruin your retinas if you aren't careful with your prescription. My hearing is fine. I don't sense anything supernatural or... or abnormal. I just read the data. And the data is sitting right there in the open, in the company database, proving exactly what they are doing to my queue. I don't need to make things up or hallucinate when the actual, physical reality of the situation is already so incredibly obvious.
Do you think it’s possible that your supervisor and the compliance team are not actually targeting you?

Is it possible? Doctor... I mean, with all due respect, did you hear what I was explaining earlier? No. No, it is absolutely not possible. 

I know I keep coming back to this, but it is because it is the absolute crux of the whole situation. Like I said, I have spent over a year—fourteen months of my life, losing sleep, stressing out—just begging for someone, anyone, to look at this objectively and take it seriously. If it were just a coincidence, if they were not actually targeting me, the math just would not add up. 

Let me break it down for you again, because you really have to understand the mechanics of this. You have the new ticket rotation on one hand, and then you have these supposedly random security audits on the other. If it were just normal business operations, the distribution of critical severity tickets would be even across the entire support team. But it is not. They are deliberately using that ticket rotation and those relentless audits to build a very specific paper trail against me. It is a manufactured narrative of incompetence, designed to give them cause for termination. 

And I have confronted them about it. I have sat in those suffocating little glass conference rooms with management, and I have laid it all out. And what do they do? Exactly what I told you before. They pull up these perfectly curated, sanitized logs, they point at the metrics on the monitor, and they give me that condescending corporate smile and tell me it is just policy. They say it is just the system functioning normally. They use those logs as a shield. But anyone who actually understands network load balancing and administrative privileges knows you can manipulate those logs to show whatever you want if you control the backend parameters. 

So, no, I do not think it is possible I am mistaken. I am not a paranoid person, I am an analyst. I analyze data. And the data shows a coordinated effort to force me out, disguised as standard operating procedure. I just... I really need someone to look past their excuses and see the paper trail for what it really is, because it is exhausting trying to fight an entire compliance team on your own.
Have you ever been able to consider that this belief might be wrong?

Doctor, I... I feel like we are going in circles here. You're basically asking me the exact same thing again, just using different words. 

Look, the entire reason I’m even here in this office, sitting in this chair talking to you today, is because for over a year now, I’ve been trying to get someone—anyone at all—to actually take this seriously. I am exhausted. I have been trying to explain to HR, to upper management, and now to you, that the new ticket rotation and these endless, targeted security audits are being used to build a paper trail against me at work. 

And it is incredibly frustrating to be asked if I might be wrong, because every time I try to sound the alarm, what happens? Management calls me in, they keep showing me those manipulated logs on their screens, and they just keep saying it’s just policy. They hide behind the word 'policy' like it's some kind of magic shield that makes what they're doing okay. 'Oh, it's just the new policy, it's just the algorithm.' 

How can I possibly sit here and consider that I might be wrong when I am watching them execute this plan day in and day out? It would be like... well, it would be like looking at a server rack that is literally on fire, smelling the smoke, watching the plastic casing melt, and having someone ask me, 'Well, have you considered that maybe the server isn't on fire?' No! Because I can see the flames! I can't just pretend the data isn't there just to make everyone else comfortable. I can't just nod and agree with my supervisor when he points at a log file that I know for a fact has been configured to hide the backend routing rules. 

You don't survive in network administration for three decades by second-guessing raw data. The evidence is the evidence. So, no, I haven't entertained the idea that I'm wrong, because I'm not. I just need someone to finally look at the facts and listen to me instead of constantly asking if I'm confused.
Is this work situation connected in any way to a police, court, or legal case?

Police? Court? No, no, it hasn't gone that far. Not yet, anyway. 

You see, Doctor, companies like this—especially when you are dealing with enterprise-level IT infrastructure and corporate liability—they do everything in their power to keep things strictly internal. They don't want the police involved. They certainly don't want a messy public lawsuit or some kind of tribunal. That is exactly why they have the compliance team and HR working in tandem to build this paper trail in the first place. 

Think about it from their perspective. If they just fired me outright without cause after thirty years in the industry, sure, I could easily get an employment lawyer. I could take them to court, and during discovery, my lawyer could subpoena the raw server logs. And believe me, if an independent forensic data analyst got their hands on those backend logs, they would see the exact same manipulated ticket assignments and targeted routing rules that I have been telling you about. The whole house of cards would collapse. 

But management isn't stupid. They know exactly how legal discovery works. So they use the new ticket rotation and these supposedly random security audits to make it look like a standard performance issue. It is a completely closed loop. HR handles it, the compliance team signs off on the sanitized metrics, and the legal system never has to know a thing. It never reaches a judge. 

So, no, there are no police involved. No active lawsuits. Just me, sitting in those suffocating little glass conference rooms, trying to defend my livelihood against a fabricated corporate narrative. I have thought about going to a lawyer, of course I have. I have spent hours, whole weekends on my days off, researching wrongful termination precedents in the tech sector, looking at how courts handle algorithmic bias in employee management. But without administrative access to the backend routing parameters to prove those logs they keep showing me are sanitized... well, it's just my word against a massive HR department. So it stays internal. They are very, very careful to keep it out of the courts.
Has this kind of work-related belief or conflict affected your relationships or behavior with people outside of work as well?

Outside of work? No, no. I mean... people assume that if you're dealing with a massive, coordinated campaign against your livelihood, your whole life must be falling apart, right? Like you're just sitting in the dark letting the mail pile up and alienating everyone around you. But that is absolutely not the case with me. 

If you look outside of this whole... this entire manufactured issue with the ticket rotation and the audits, everything else is perfectly fine. I still keep my house in complete order. Just last weekend, I spent four hours cleaning out the gutters and reorganizing the workbench in the garage because I like things to be structured. I manage all our finances, the bills are paid on time every single month, down to the exact cent. I help my wife out around the house, we run our errands together, we have dinner every night. My relationship with her is solid. She knows how much stress I'm under with this whole compliance team nightmare, but I don't let it destroy our home life. I wouldn't let them take that from me.

And frankly, even at the office, if you strip away their interference, I handle the technical parts of my job flawlessly. I really do. Nobody—not even my supervisor, as much as he wants me gone—can look me in the eye and say my actual work is sloppy. They can't say I'm disorganized. When I configure a network switch or troubleshoot a legacy server, it is done right the first time. My code is clean, my documentation is meticulous. 

That is exactly why they have to rely on manipulating those ticket metrics, Doctor. Don't you see how it all connects? If I were actually disorganized, if my personal life were a mess, if I were forgetting to pay my bills or slacking off on the technical side of my job, they wouldn't need to build this fake paper trail. They could just fire me for genuine poor performance. But because I keep my house in order, because I am a reliable husband to my wife, and because my technical work is absolutely unimpeachable... they have to invent a reason. So, no, my behavior outside of this specific targeting hasn't deteriorated at all. I am as disciplined as I have ever been.
Have you always been the kind of person who prefers to keep to yourself rather than having close relationships?

Keep to myself? No, no, not at all. I mean, I know exactly what you're getting at with a question like that. There is this incredibly pervasive stereotype about IT guys, especially guys from my generation who started out back in the early Novell NetWare and legacy mainframe days, that we're all just... I don't know, anti-social hermits sitting in a dark basement who would rather talk to a motherboard than a human being. But that has never been me. Never. 

I have been married for thirty-two years, Doctor. You simply don't sustain a marriage for three decades by being a recluse who can't handle close relationships. My wife and I, we actually have a very solid circle of friends. We host a neighborhood barbecue every single Fourth of July—and I don't just mean throwing some hot dogs on a grill, I mean I am the one who organizes the whole thing. I coordinate with the HOA, I get the street closure permits filed weeks in advance, I drive three towns over to a specific butcher because he's the only one who trims the brisket exactly the way it needs to be for a twelve-hour smoke. I enjoy doing that. I enjoy the camaraderie. 

And even at work, before this whole... before this targeted campaign started with the compliance team and the HR audits, I was always very engaged with my colleagues. Back in the early 2000s, I actually ran the department's softball team. I kept the roster, I organized the practice schedules, I collected the dues for the uniforms. I have always valued clear, honest communication with the people around me. 

Which, frankly, is exactly why this current situation at the office is so incredibly maddening to me! I am trying to communicate with them. I am trying to have a transparent, professional dialogue about these sanitized logs and the backend routing rules, and *they* are the ones shutting me out. They are the ones isolating me, stonewalling me, and refusing to have a real conversation. If I were actually a loner, if I were the kind of guy who just wanted to be left alone, maybe I wouldn't even care. Maybe I would just put my head down, ignore the manipulated ticket queues, and collect my paycheck. But because I actually care about the integrity of my work and my relationships with management, I am speaking up. 

So I really don't see why my social preferences are even on the table here. I don't prefer to be alone. I am just being forced into a corner by a group of people who refuse to look at the raw data.
Do you feel distrustful or suspicious of most people in your life, not just people at work?

Distrustful? Of most people? No, no, absolutely not. I think... I think you might be fundamentally misunderstanding the scope of what I'm dealing with here, Doctor. I am not walking around looking over my shoulder at the grocery store. I don't think the mailman is out to get me. 

Take my mechanic, for example. Dave, down at the shop on 4th Street. I've been taking my vehicles to him for, gosh, it has to be fifteen years now. When Dave calls me up and says the timing belt on the Honda is wearing thin and needs to be replaced, I don't demand to see his diagnostic readouts. I don't accuse him of fabricating a mechanical issue just to pad his invoice. I just say, "Okay, Dave, go ahead and fix it," because we have mutual trust. Or my neighbor, Tom. Tom borrowed my heavy-duty pressure washer a couple of weeks ago to do his driveway. Am I sitting by the front window, peeking through the blinds, wondering if Tom is secretly plotting to keep my equipment forever? Of course not. That would be completely irrational. 

I trust my wife implicitly. I trust my friends. I trust the guy at the hardware store when he tells me which sealant to buy. 

The only people I do not trust—and I really need to emphasize this, because this isn't some vague, generalized suspicion, this is based on concrete, empirical observation—are the people in management and HR who are actively manipulating the enterprise routing algorithms to push me out. If my supervisor were just a normal guy giving me honest, objective feedback, I would trust him too! But when he hands me a quarterly review claiming my ticket resolution time has dropped by forty percent, and I know for a fact that the backend system was deliberately reconfigured to dump all the high-latency Tier 3 legacy server failures directly into my queue exactly three weeks before the compliance audit... well, trusting him wouldn't just be naive, it would be professional suicide. 

So, no. I don't have a problem trusting people in my life. I don't walk around with a chip on my shoulder. I just have a problem with a very specific, coordinated group of people who are falsifying administrative data to ruin my career. There is a massive difference between being a suspicious person and simply paying attention to the parameters right in front of you.
Have you always believed that the people around you might be misleading or taking advantage of you?

Always? No, definitely not. I mean, that would be exhausting, wouldn't it? Walking through your whole life assuming everyone has an angle. No, if you look at my track record, my career history, I have always been a very trusting person. Probably too trusting, if I’m being perfectly honest. 

Take my first major corporate job. This was back in the late eighties, early nineties, right when enterprise networking was really starting to take off. I worked under a regional IT director named... well, his name was Gordon. Gordon was old-school. If he told you something, you could take it to the bank. I remember when we were doing a massive migration from token-ring networks over to Ethernet—this was a huge, multi-month project across three different office buildings, pulling cables through drop ceilings at two in the morning, weekend after weekend. Gordon would say, "I need this subnet configured by Monday," and I would just do it, and when the project succeeded, he made sure I got the credit. I never once thought Gordon was trying to pull one over on me. I never thought he was secretly trying to sabotage my performance reviews or take advantage of my late hours. We had a great working relationship. 

And it was like that for decades! Through the dot-com bubble, through all the Y2K preparations—which, by the way, I spearheaded for a logistics company down in the valley, working eighty-hour weeks because I believed in the company's mission and I trusted the executives when they said we’d be compensated for the overtime. And we were! They paid out the bonuses exactly as promised. I never doubted them for a second.

So, no, I don't have this... this lifelong complex about people taking advantage of me. I really don't. I am a systems guy, Doctor. I look at inputs and outputs. For the vast majority of my life, the inputs from the people around me have been honest, and so my output has been trust. 

It is only *this* specific group of people, *this* current compliance team and my current supervisor, who have altered the variables. They are the ones who started quietly re-routing the high-latency tickets to my queue. They are the ones who started locking me out of the administrative dashboards so I couldn't pull the raw server logs to prove what they were doing. 

If I had always believed people were out to get me, I wouldn't have lasted thirty-five years in corporate IT. I would have burned out in my twenties. The only reason I'm raising red flags now is because the evidence in front of me is undeniable. It's not a personality trait of mine to be suspicious. It's just... well, it's just basic situational awareness. When a specific group of people is actively holding a match to your career, you don't just close your eyes and pretend you don't smell smoke, you know?
Do you think there is any chance at all that your supervisor is not intentionally targeting you?

Any chance at all? Look, Doctor... I mean, I wish there was. I really, genuinely do. It would make my life a whole lot easier if this was just some giant misunderstanding, some... some glitch in the automated assignment rules, so to speak. But no. No, there is absolutely zero chance this is unintentional, and I'll tell you exactly why. 

The whole reason I am even sitting here talking to you today, the entire reason I'm here, is because for over a year now—well over twelve months, probably closer to fourteen or fifteen if we go back to when the first firewall rules were quietly modified—I have been trying, practically begging, to get someone, *anyone*, to take seriously what is actually happening to me. They implemented this new ticket rotation system, right? And right alongside it, they rolled out these so-called random security audits. And if you just look at the surface, if you aren't a systems guy who knows how the backend architecture operates, maybe you'd think, "Oh, it's just administrative bloat, it's just corporate restructuring." 

But it’s not. It is a highly calculated, systematic effort, and these ticket rotations and security audits are being used to build a paper trail against me at work. They are manufacturing a documented history of latency and incompetence that doesn't actually exist in reality! And the most frustrating part, the part that just makes my blood boil and keeps me up at night, is that whenever I bring this up, whenever I escalate it to the director level, management just puts on these polite faces and keeps showing me these sanitized server logs. They point to the printouts and they say, "Oh, look, it's just the new policy, it's just the automated rotation doing its job." 

"It’s just policy." That's their favorite line. Even though management keeps showing me logs and saying it's just policy, it is so painfully obvious to me what they are doing. They act as if I haven't spent my entire adult life writing and troubleshooting the exact kind of routing policies they're hiding behind! I know what a manipulated log looks like. I know when an audit is being weaponized to target one specific employee. 

So, no, Doctor, I don't think there is any chance my supervisor is just accidentally destroying my career. When you look at the sheer volume of evidence I've compiled over the last year, it is entirely, one hundred percent intentional.
How certain are you, right now, that your supervisor is intentionally targeting you?

I am one hundred percent certain. Beyond a shadow of a doubt. I mean, like I was just trying to explain to you a second ago, Doctor—this isn't some hunch. I wouldn't be sitting in this chair, taking up your time and mine, if I wasn't absolutely positive. 

The entire reason I am here today is because I have spent over a year, day in and day out, trying to get someone... anyone at all... to take this seriously. I've been practically shouting it from the rooftops! They are using this new ticket rotation system, along with those supposedly random security audits, to meticulously build a paper trail against me at work. That is a fact. They are manufacturing a reason to terminate me. 

And I know I just mentioned the server logs, but you have to understand how incredibly maddening it is to deal with this day after day. Every single time I try to expose what they're doing, every time I bring the actual data to them, management just pulls up those same sanitized logs. They point at the printouts, they give me this condescending little corporate smile, and they say, "Oh, it's just the new policy, it's just the automated system doing what it's supposed to do." 

Just policy! They hide behind that word like a shield. It's the perfect cover for them, because to anyone else, it just looks like routine administrative bureaucracy. But I know better.
